defect: I ran scripts/validate_staging_artifact.py five times while concurrently rewriting the files it reads. A validator racing its writer can report a PASS on a byte state that never existed as a whole.
why_it_matters: this is MEMORY.md's 'parallel agents must not share one .next' lesson, committed against my own gate -- which is worse than committing it against a build, because the gate is the instrument that is supposed to catch me. A PASS obtained this way is not evidence about the artifact; it is evidence about whatever mixture of old and new bytes the run happened to read.
how_it_was_caught: comparing each run's manifest.file_checksums count against the file count actually on disk. Five runs reported 28/28 while the shipped manifest lists 29.

timeline.note: started 8 seconds after the last staging write, on a directory frozen for its whole run

resolution: all five racing PASSes are WITHDRAWN as evidence about this artifact. The verdict of record is bqvgkdaqs: 29/29 checksums, 17 checks, 11,181 rows, 100% evaluation coverage on every check, PASS.
the_rule_this_should_have_followed: the manifest is generated LAST, and nothing writes to the staging directory between manifest generation and the validation that covers it. The checksum count in a run's output is the cheap way to tell which byte state a verdict describes, and it should be read every time rather than the word PASS.
